Chapter 2 Stress and equilibrium

2.7 Equilibrium of a small box

All three questions with which section 2.6 ended are about the stress at a single point. First, though, we must look at how the stresses at neighbouring points are related to each other. We will need this in every body in which we look for the stresses, and on the same small piece of a body we will answer the third question in the next section.

Can the stress change from point to point in any way at all? No. Let us cut a small piece out of a body in thought. The body is in equilibrium, so this piece is in equilibrium too (section 2.1). On it act the forces across its faces, which are set by the traction vectors on the faces, and the forces that act on all of its matter, like the weight. If the traction vectors on every pair of opposite faces were exactly opposite, all the forces across the faces would balance each other, and nothing would carry the weight of the piece. So the stress must change in at least one direction, and the differences of the forces across all three pairs of faces together carry the weight. For the slice of the hanging bar below we will see this with numbers: the force on the top face is larger than the force on the bottom face by exactly the weight of the slice.

Let us draw what it means that the traction vectors on a pair of opposite faces are exactly opposite. Figure 2.80 shows the same small cube around the point \(P\) from two sides. In the left picture we look at it as in figure 2.74, from the side to which the axes point. We see the three faces with the outward normals \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) and on each of them the three components of its traction vector. In the right picture we have walked around the cube and look at it from the opposite corner, from behind and from below, so the axis \(x\) points away from us and the axis \(y\) to the left. We see the other three faces, with the outward normals \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). Suppose the stress on both faces of every pair is the same as at the point \(P\). The traction vector on the face with the normal \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) is then \(-\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\), by lemma 2.21 on the traction on the opposite side of a cut, so its three components are drawn in the negative directions of the axes. The normal component \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) points in the direction of the axis \(x\) in the left picture and in the direction \(-x\) in the right one, both times out of the cube. \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) points in the direction of the axis \(y\) in the left picture and in the direction \(-y\) in the right one, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) up on the left and down on the right. It is the same with the components on the faces perpendicular to the axis \(y\) and with the components on the faces perpendicular to the axis \(z\). Each of the nine arrows on the left has a twin on the right, equally long and pointing the opposite way. The two faces of a pair have the same area, so all nine pairs of forces cancel. This is the case in which nothing carries the weight. In a cube that carries its own weight, at least one arrow in the right picture must therefore have a different length from its twin on the left.

From history

On 14 May 1821 Navier presented to the Paris Academy a memoir on the equilibrium and motion of solid bodies that return to their original shape after unloading (TIMO, PDF p. 113). He saw the body, as we said in chapter 1, as a set of particles with forces acting between them (figure 1.7). These are proportional to the change of distance between two particles and directed along the line joining them (TIMO, PDF p. 113). He added up the forces of all the particles in the neighbourhood of one particle and wrote the condition that together with an external force, for example weight, they are in equilibrium (TIMO, PDF p. 113 and 114). LOVE counts Navier's general equations of 1821 as one of the two greatest landmarks of the theory, besides Hooke's proportionality of force and extension (chapter 1), since with them all questions about small changes of shape were reduced to calculation (LOVE, PDF p. 19). Cauchy read Navier's memoir and began to work on the same question (TIMO, PDF p. 116). Instead of forces between particles he took the pressure on a surface, which he knew from hydrodynamics, and allowed that in a solid it need not be perpendicular to the surface (chapter 1, TIMO, PDF p. 116). He presented his work to the Academy on 30 September 1822 (TIMO, PDF p. 116). By the autumn of that year he had derived, for a small box, the equations of equilibrium that connect the stresses with the force per unit volume (LOVE, PDF p. 25, TIMO, PDF p. 117).

In deriving the equilibrium of a small piece of a body the forces between particles need not be known, the forces across the faces of the piece suffice. We shall follow the same path.

The goal of this section is to write this condition with numbers. For every interior point of a body we will derive three equations between the partial derivatives of the stress components and the force per unit volume that acts on the matter. The route is similar to the one for Cauchy's formula. First we write the condition for a slice of the hanging bar, where everything is simple and exact. Then we say exactly what a force that acts on all the matter of a body is. Then we cut a small cube out of a general body, write its equilibrium, divide it by the volume of the cube and let the cube shrink to a point. For this step we will need one more small tool from mathematics. Finally we test the equations on the hanging bar, on pure shear and on water at rest.

We will use only the first condition of equilibrium from definition 2.3, that the resultant of the forces is the zero vector. The second condition, that the forces do not turn the body, comes in the next section. As so far in this chapter, we do not distinguish the shape of the body before and after loading. In steel, which deforms by less than a thousandth, an edge of a cube with side 1 mm changes under loading by less than 1 µm. The area of a face of the cube therefore changes by at most about 0,2 %, and by that much we can be wrong in the forces across the faces if we compute them with the areas before loading. In rubber, which stretches by several tens of percent, the error would be of the same order, tens of percent, and there the assumption does not hold. CM derives these equations in the same way and assumes small deformations explicitly (CM §4.5, PDF p. 198). What changes for large deformations we will see at the end of the chapter.

2.7.1 Why two pieces: the tetrahedron and the cube

Why did we cut a tetrahedron out of the body for Cauchy's formula, while here we will cut a cube? The two pieces answer different questions, and each has the shape its question demands (figure 2.82). At the top is the body. On a part of its surface pushes the load \(\bar{\vek t}\), a force per unit area that we know.

The cube is cut from the interior of the body and drawn enlarged at the bottom left. All six of its faces are cuts through the matter, so we know the traction vector on none of them. But the cube has three pairs of parallel faces. On the right and the left face the traction vectors \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}})\) and \(\vek t(-\vek e_{\mathrm{y}})\) are nearly opposite, as in figure 2.80. As much as they differ, so much the stress changes on the way from one face to the other. These differences must be balanced by the body force \(\vek b\), the force on all the matter of the cube, like the weight. From this we will get equations that hold at every interior point of the body. A tetrahedron has not a single pair of parallel faces, so no such difference can be written on it.

The tetrahedron, however, has the slanted face \(ABC\), for which we can choose any normal \(\vek n\). The cube has only six normals, all along the axes. That is why the tetrahedron gave us Cauchy's formula. Its slanted face has a second role as well. We can cut the tetrahedron right at the surface of the body, so that the face \(ABC\) is a piece of the surface itself (bottom right), while the three faces through the point \(P\) are cuts in the interior. On \(ABC\) then acts not the rest of the body but the load, which we know. The equilibrium of the tetrahedron is the same as in section 2.6.2, only the traction vector on the slanted face is now known. By Cauchy's formula (2.25) the stress components just below the surface must therefore give exactly the load:

\[n_{\mathrm{x}}\,\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) + n_{\mathrm{y}}\,\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}) + n_{\mathrm{z}}\,\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}) = \bar{\vek t} .\]

On the hanging bar of figure 2.84 we know this already. The lower end of the bar is free, there \(\vek n = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\bar{\vek t} = \vek 0\), so \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) = \vek 0\) and the stress is \(\sigma(L) = 0\). On the top face \(\vek n = -\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), and the load pulls up with \(0{,}765\) MPa, so \(-\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) = -0{,}765\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) MPa and \(\sigma(0) = 0{,}765\) MPa. The mantle of the bar is parallel to the axis \(x\), so on it \(\vek n = (0, n_{\mathrm{y}}, n_{\mathrm{z}})\), and nothing acts on it, \(\bar{\vek t} = \vek 0\). The condition \(n_{\mathrm{y}}\,\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}) + n_{\mathrm{z}}\,\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}) = \vek 0\) holds, since \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}) = \vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}) = \vek 0\) in the bar.

Here we assumed two things that theorem 2.26 does not cover, since there \(P\) is an interior point. First, that the piece of surface \(ABC\) is flat. A smooth surface is nearly flat on a small enough piece. On the mantle of the bar with radius 5 mm the normal turns over a piece 0,01 mm wide by only \(0{,}01/5 = 0{,}002\) rad. As the piece shrinks, this turn goes to zero, so the assumption of a flat piece brings no error in the limit. At an edge or a corner of a body, however, a single normal does not exist, and there we write the condition for each face separately, as above for the bottom face and the mantle of the bar. Second, that the stress components do not change by a jump as we approach the surface from the interior. If they did, the formula would connect the load with the stress on the surface itself and would say nothing about the interior just below it. A jump occurs, for example, at the joint of two materials that reaches the surface, or under the edge of a rigid body pressed into the surface. We will state both assumptions exactly in chapter 11 (definition 11.1, conditions 2 and 3), and there the condition on the surface will be called the boundary condition (SADD §5.2, PDF p. 104). So the work is divided: the cube gives the equations for the interior, and the tetrahedron at the surface says how the stress in the interior meets the load.

Where did the weight go in the tetrahedron? It appeared in its equilibrium but dropped out in the limit, because the volume of the tetrahedron shrinks faster than the areas of its faces (section 2.6.2). In the lectures the equilibrium of the tetrahedron is therefore written without the body force from the start, and the result is the same. For the cube it will be different. The forces on a pair of opposite faces nearly cancel, and what remains of them is as small as the weight: both are proportional to the volume of the cube. So we will divide the equilibrium of the cube by the volume, not by the area, and the body force will stay in the equations.

One more remark on Cauchy's formula. It contains the traction vectors on three planes perpendicular to the axes. Any three planes through \(P\) whose normals do not lie in one plane would serve just as well. In the lectures these are three traction vectors with linearly independent normals. We will meet this notion for general vectors in chapter 6. Three such planes form a corner, like the three faces through \(P\), a fourth face closes it into a tetrahedron, and the argument of section 2.6.2 goes through. Let us test this at the top of the hanging bar, where \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) = (765, 0, 0)\) kPa and \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}) = \vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}) = \vek 0\). Suppose that instead we know the traction vectors for the normals \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek n_2 = (1, 1, 0)/\sqrt 2\) and \(\vek n_3 = (1, 0, 1)/\sqrt 2\) (figure 2.83, left). The planes with these normals form a corner at the point \(P\), which the face \(ABC\) closes into a tetrahedron. The traction vectors on them all point in the direction of the axis \(x\):

\[\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) = (765, 0, 0)\ \text{kPa} , \qquad \vek t(\vek n_2) = \vek t(\vek n_3) = (765/\sqrt 2,\ 0,\ 0)\ \text{kPa} \approx (541, 0, 0)\ \text{kPa} .\]

By Cauchy's formula \(\vek t(\vek n_2) = \big(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) + \vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}})\big)/\sqrt 2\), so

\[\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}) = \sqrt 2\,\vek t(\vek n_2) - \vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) = (765 - 765,\ 0,\ 0)\ \text{kPa} = \vek 0 ,\]

and in the same way \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}) = \sqrt 2\,\vek t(\vek n_3) - \vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) = \vek 0\). We have recovered all three vectors of the formula. The normals \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \((1, 1, 0)/\sqrt 2\), on the other hand, lie in one plane (figure 2.83, right). The traction vector for the third is \(\big(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) + \vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}})\big)/\sqrt 2\), so we compute it from the first two and it says nothing new, and about \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}})\) we learn nothing. Three such planes share a line, here the axis \(z\), and do not form a corner that a fourth face could close: the space between two sheets extends up and down along the axis \(z\) without end, and a fourth plane cuts it off on one side only.

2.7.2 A slice of the hanging bar

Let us return to the goal of the section, the equilibrium of a small piece inside a body, and start with an example we know. The steel hanging bar has the length \(L = 10\) m, a round cross section with diameter 10 mm and area \(A = 7{,}854 \cdot 10^{-5}\ \text{m}^2\), and the density of steel is \(\rho = 7800\) kg/m³. The bar hangs under its own weight and is held in the idealized way of section 1.7.1: only the centre of the top face is fixed, and the weight is carried by a force that pulls the top face up evenly. The axis \(x\) points vertically down from the centre of the top face. In section 2.2 we found from the equilibrium of the lower part of the bar the stress in the cross section at the depth \(x\),

\[\sigma(x) = \rho g\,(L - x) ,\]

the same at all points of the cross section (equation (2.5)).

Now let us go the other way: we do not know the stress, we know only the weight. We assume only, as everywhere for bars, that on the cross section at the depth \(x\) the traction vector for the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) is \(\sigma(x)\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) at all points of the cross section, but we do not know the function \(\sigma\). We cut the bar in thought by the cross sections at the depths \(x - \tfrac{\Delta x}{2}\) and \(x + \tfrac{\Delta x}{2}\) and look at the slice (rezina) between them, of thickness \(\Delta x\), with its centre at the depth \(x\) (figure 2.84). Every slice of the bar can be described in this way by its centre and its thickness. In the figure the bar on the left is a rectangle with the axis \(x\), the small arrows at the top are the force that pulls the bar up evenly at its top, \(L\) is its length, the depth \(x\) is the distance from the top to the centre of the slice, and the blue slice is the piece we look at. In the middle the slice is enlarged, with its thickness \(\Delta x\). Which forces act on it?

  1. Across the top face the part of the bar above pulls it. The outward normal of the slice is \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) there, so by lemma 2.21 on the traction on the opposite side of a cut the traction vector there is \(-\sigma(x - \tfrac{\Delta x}{2})\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). It is the same at all points of the face, so the force is the area times it, \(-\sigma(x - \tfrac{\Delta x}{2})\,A\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). It points up.
  2. Across the bottom face, with outward normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), the part of the bar below pulls it with the force \(\sigma(x + \tfrac{\Delta x}{2})\,A\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), which points down.
  3. The mantle of the slice, its side surface, is part of the surface of the bar, on which nothing acts.
  4. The slice has the volume \(A\,\Delta x\), the mass \(\rho A\,\Delta x\) and by (2.1) the weight \(\rho g A\,\Delta x\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), which points down.
  5. The slice is in equilibrium, so by (2.2) the sum of these forces is the zero vector: the force at the top and the weight point opposite to the force at the bottom. All the forces point along the axis \(x\), so we write only the component \(x\):
    \[-\sigma(x - \tfrac{\Delta x}{2})\,A + \sigma(x + \tfrac{\Delta x}{2})\,A + \rho g A\,\Delta x = 0 .\]
  6. We divide the equation by the volume of the slice \(A\,\Delta x\):
    \[\frac{\sigma(x + \tfrac{\Delta x}{2}) - \sigma(x - \tfrac{\Delta x}{2})}{\Delta x} + \rho g = 0 . \tag{2.28}\]

The equation says that the stress on the bottom face of the slice is smaller than on the top face, and that the difference, divided by the thickness of the slice, is exactly the weight per unit volume, \(\rho g\). Why? The part of the bar above the slice must carry everything that the part below carries, and the weight of the slice besides. We made this argument already for the piece of a bar in figure 1.25. For steel

\[\rho g = 7800\ \frac{\text{kg}}{\text{m}^3} \cdot 9{,}81\ \frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}^2} = 76\,518\ \frac{\text{N}}{\text{m}^3} ,\]

so the stress falls by 76 518 Pa, that is by \(0{,}0765\) MPa, for every metre of depth. Over the 10 m from the top to the bottom this gives \(0{,}765\) MPa, exactly the stress at the top from section 2.2. Figure 2.84 shows the forces to scale for the slice from the depth \(2L/5\) to the depth \(3L/5\). It is pulled up by the force \(36{,}06\) N and down by \(24{,}04\) N, its weight is \(12{,}02\) N, and indeed \(36{,}06 = 24{,}04 + 12{,}02\). On the right is the graph of the stress \(\sigma(x) = \rho g\,(L - x)\): the straight line falls from \(\rho g L\) at the top to zero at \(x = L\), and between the depths \(x - \Delta x/2\) and \(x + \Delta x/2\) it falls by \(\rho g\,\Delta x\).

Let us check the equation with the stress \(\sigma(x) = \rho g\,(L - x)\). The numerator in (2.28) is the difference of the stresses between the two depths

\[\sigma(x + \tfrac{\Delta x}{2}) - \sigma(x - \tfrac{\Delta x}{2}) = \rho g\,(L - x - \tfrac{\Delta x}{2}) - \rho g\,(L - x + \tfrac{\Delta x}{2}) = -\rho g\,\Delta x ,\]

and divided by \(\Delta x\) it gives \(-\rho g\). Equation (2.28) holds for every thickness of the slice, not only for a small one, because in the bar the stress is the same over every cross section and nothing acts on the mantle. So it even gives us the stress itself. Take the slice from any depth \(x_1\) to the lower end of the bar. The bottom face of this slice is the free end of the bar, where the line reaches zero, \(\sigma(L) = 0\). By (2.28) the difference of the stresses divided by the thickness is \(-\rho g\):

\[\frac{0 - \sigma(x_1)}{L - x_1} = -\rho g , \qquad \text{so} \qquad \sigma(x_1) = \rho g\,(L - x_1) .\]

This is the same calculation as in section 2.1, only written with the stress.

And when the slice is very thin? The first term of (2.28) is the difference of the values of the function \(\sigma\) at two points that lie symmetrically about \(x\), which is the drop of the stress, divided by the distance between them. Below we will show that such a quotient approaches the derivative \(\sigma'(x)\) as \(\Delta x\) goes to zero. The equation then reads \(\sigma'(x) + \rho g = 0\): the rate at which the stress changes with depth and the weight per unit volume add up to zero. This form no longer speaks about a slice but about a single depth \(x\). We will get exactly this form in a general body. There, however, is more work. The stress changes also over the faces of a piece, forces act across all of its faces, not only across two, and they do not point only along one axis. Before we take this on, let us say exactly what a force is that acts, like the weight, on all the matter.

2.7.3 Body force

The weight of the slice was proportional to its volume: \(\rho g\) times the volume. The weight acts on every bit of matter separately, not only on the surface of the body. A force with this property has its own name in books, as we mentioned already in section 1.2. A force that acts only on the surface of a body, for example the pull of a rope or the push of water on a wall, is a surface force (površinska sila) (SADD §3.1, PDF p. 63). A surface force at a point of the surface is described by the traction vector, the force per unit area (section 2.5). A force that acts on all the matter is described in a similar way, by the force per unit volume. For the traction vector we shrank patches around the point, here we will shrink cubes. Figure 2.85 shows both kinds of force. On the left the body lies on two supports. The blue arrows are the weight, which acts on every bit of its matter, and the arrows from below are the forces of the supports, which push only on the surface. The load that pushes from above acts only on the surface too. Around the point \(P\) is a grey frame, which is enlarged on the right: the cube with the centre \(P\), the side \(h\) and the body force \(\Delta\vek F_{\mathrm{V}}\) on its matter.

Definition 2.28 Body force (prostorninska sila)

A body force (prostorninska sila) is a force with which something outside a body acts on all of its matter, on every bit of it separately, unlike forces that push only on the surface. Let \(P\) be an interior point of the body and \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) the axes of a rectangular Cartesian coordinate system. For \(h > 0\) let \(\Delta\vek F_{\mathrm{V}}\) be the body force on the matter in the cube with centre \(P\), side \(h\) and edges parallel to the axes. The body force density (gostota prostorninske sile) at the point \(P\) is the vector

\[\vek b(P) = \lim_{\mathrm{h} \to 0^+} \frac{\Delta\vek F_{\mathrm{V}}}{h^3} , \tag{2.29}\]

if this limit from the right (definition 1.8) exists. The limit of a vector is taken component by component.

Source: SADD §3.1, (3.1.1) (PDF p. 63), BOWER §2.2.1 (PDF pp. 66-67), CM §5.3.1.1, (5.3.4) (PDF pp. 226-227). BOWER writes the force per unit mass with a limit but does not give the shape of the pieces. SADD and CM introduce the density as a function from which the force on a part of the body follows by summation over its volume. The shrinking cubes are not from the sources.

The number \(h^3\) is the volume of the cube with side \(h\), so \(\Delta\vek F_{\mathrm{V}}/h^3\) is the average force per unit volume in the cube, just as \(\Delta\vek F/\Delta A\) was the average force per unit area on a patch. As we shrink the cube around \(P\), the average approaches the force per unit volume at the point \(P\). The unit is N/m³. The point must be interior so that for small \(h\) the whole cube lies in the body. We chose cubes because we will need them in the equilibrium below. The exact summation over the volume, by which SADD and CM introduce the density (the box of sources above), we will meet in chapter 4.

Let us test the definition on the weight. Let the body have the same density \(\rho\) everywhere. A cube with side \(h\) has the mass \(\rho h^3\) and by (2.1) a weight of magnitude \(\rho g h^3\), pointing down. If the axis \(x\) points down, as for the hanging bar, then \(\Delta\vek F_{\mathrm{V}} = \rho g h^3\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and

\[\frac{\Delta\vek F_{\mathrm{V}}}{h^3} = \rho g\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\]

for every \(h\). The quotient is the same vector for all cubes, so its limit is this vector too: \(\vek b = \rho g\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). For steel its magnitude is \(76\,518\) N/m³. A cube of steel with side 1 cm has the volume \(10^{-6}\) m³ and weighs \(0{,}0765\) N. For a body with the same density everywhere we would get the same vector also if we shrank pieces of another shape. Other body forces are electric and magnetic forces (BOWER §2.2.1, PDF p. 66).

External forces are divided by a second key as well: whether we know them in advance. In figure 2.85 the weight and the load act no matter how the body is supported. These are applied forces (aktivne sile), together we call them the loading. The forces of the supports are reaction forces or reactions (reaktivne sile, reakcije). A support does not push of its own accord, but only as much as is needed to keep the body from moving. So we do not know the reactions in advance and compute them from equilibrium (GR §1.1.2, PDF pp. 33-34, where the forces on a constrained particle are separated in this way). With numbers (figure 2.86): let the body weigh 100 N and let the load push with 40 N midway between the supports. By (2.2) the supports together must push up with 140 N, and since everything is symmetric, each with 70 N. If we remove the load, the reactions drop by themselves to 50 N, while the weight stays 100 N. The two divisions are independent: the weight is an applied body force, the load an applied surface force, and the reactions of the supports are reactive surface forces.

Books write the body force in different ways. SADD writes the force per unit volume, as we do, with the letter \(\vek F\) (SADD (3.1.1), PDF p. 63). CM and BOWER write the force per unit mass, \(\vek f\) and \(\vek b\), and multiply it by the density (CM, PDF p. 226, BOWER, PDF p. 67). So our \(\vek b\) is \(\rho\,\vek f\) in CM and \(\rho\,\vek b\) in BOWER. Where there is no doubt, we also call \(\vek b\) simply the body force. The force per unit mass has the unit N/kg, which is the same as m/s². For the weight it is the acceleration of gravity \(g = 9{,}81\) N/kg for every material, while the force per unit volume depends on the material: \(76\,518\) N/m³ for steel, and \(2700 \cdot 9{,}81 = 26\,487\) N/m³ for aluminium with the density 2700 kg/m³. On cubes of the same size the arrow of the weight is therefore almost three times shorter for aluminium than for steel, \(76\,518/26\,487 = 2{,}89\).

In the lectures the body force is called telesna sila and written \(\vec f\), given per unit volume (N/m³) or per unit mass (N/kg), and the axes are \(x_1\), \(x_2\), \(x_3\).

2.7.4 Density at a point

For the weight we assumed that the body has the same density everywhere. What about a body joined from two metals? Then the mass of one cubic metre of matter is no longer one number for the whole body. So we must tie the density to a point, as we did the body force, and we use the same cubes with the centre \(P\) and the side \(h\).

Definition 2.29 Mass density at a point (gostota v točki)

Let \(P\) be an interior point of the body and \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) the axes of a rectangular Cartesian coordinate system. For \(h > 0\) let \(\Delta m\) be the mass of the matter in the cube with centre \(P\), side \(h\) and edges parallel to the axes. The mass density (gostota) at the point \(P\) is the number

\[\rho(P) = \lim_{\mathrm{h} \to 0^+} \frac{\Delta m}{h^3} , \tag{2.30}\]

if this limit from the right (definition 1.8) exists. The density of the body is the function \(\rho\) that assigns this number to every interior point at which the limit exists.

Source: EP §2.1.1, (2.1.1) (p. 47): the density as the limit of mass divided by volume as the volume goes to zero. EP does not give the shape of the pieces. The shrinking cubes are not from the source.

The quotient \(\Delta m/h^3\) is the average mass per unit volume in the cube, its unit is kg/m³. In a piece of steel alone, a cube with side 1 cm has the volume \(10^{-6}\) m³ and the mass \(7{,}8\) g, and a cube with side 1 mm has the volume \(10^{-9}\) m³ and the mass \(7{,}8\) mg. The quotient is 7800 kg/m³ both times, and so it is for every \(h\), so the limit is the same number.

Now take a piece in which steel and aluminium are joined along a plane (figure 2.88, left). We choose the axes so that the joint is perpendicular to one of them. Then two faces of every cube are parallel to the joint, in the section they are the vertical sides of the squares. The steel has the density 7800 kg/m³, the aluminium 2700 kg/m³ (BOWER, table 3.1, PDF p. 100, gives 2,6 to 2,9 Mg/m³ for aluminium and its alloys). The point \(P\) lies in the steel, 1 mm from the joint. The cube with side 10 mm reaches 5 mm to each side of \(P\), so 4 mm across the joint. Four tenths of its volume are aluminium, so

\[\frac{\Delta m}{h^3} = 0{,}6 \cdot 7800\ \frac{\text{kg}}{\text{m}^3} + 0{,}4 \cdot 2700\ \frac{\text{kg}}{\text{m}^3} = 5760\ \frac{\text{kg}}{\text{m}^3} .\]

The cube with side 4 mm reaches 1 mm across the joint, a quarter of it is aluminium, and the quotient is \(0{,}75 \cdot 7800 + 0{,}25 \cdot 2700 = 6525\) kg/m³. The cube with side 2 mm only touches the joint, and every smaller one lies entirely in the steel, so the quotient is 7800 kg/m³ for all \(h \le 2\) mm. The limit is therefore \(\rho(P) = 7800\) kg/m³. The average over a large cube says something about the neighbourhood of the point, the limit about the matter at the point itself. That is why the definition asks for a limit.

And the point \(Q\) on the joint itself (figure 2.88, right)? The cube with centre \(Q\) is half steel and half aluminium for every \(h\). The quotient is always \((7800 + 2700)/2 = 5250\) kg/m³, so the limit of the definition exists and is 5250 kg/m³. But no matter at \(Q\) has this density. If we shrank cubes that touch the joint from the steel side, we would get 7800 kg/m³, and from the aluminium side 2700 kg/m³. Here the number depends on how we place the cubes, so on the joint we do not use the density at a point and speak of the density on each side separately. At \(P\) it is different: every small enough piece around \(P\) lies entirely in the steel and gives 7800 kg/m³, however we place it.

And if the joint is perpendicular to none of the axes (figure 2.89)? Then the shares of aluminium in the large cubes differ, but the limit is the same. The point \(P\) is 1 mm from the oblique joint, so the ball with centre \(P\) and radius 1 mm lies in the steel and only touches the joint. The points of the cube farthest from \(P\) are its corners, at the ends of the space diagonal. We see them in the section through two opposite edges, where the cube is a rectangle with sides \(h\) and \(\sqrt2\,h\). By Pythagoras' theorem its diagonal is \(\sqrt{h^2 + 2h^2} = \sqrt3\,h\), so the corner is \(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}h\) from \(P\). For \(h < 1\) mm this is less than \(0{,}866\) mm, so the whole cube is inside the ball and therefore in the steel, however the joint is tilted and however we choose the axes. The quotient is 7800 kg/m³ for all such \(h\).

The limit holds for the continuous matter of chapter 1 (figure 1.4), in which a cube can be shrunk without end. Real matter must not be shrunk down to the atoms: a cube with a side below a nanometre holds only a handful of atoms or none, and the quotient jumps when we move the cube a little. So the picture of continuous matter may fail at the scale of a nanometre (EP, p. 47). We may use the assumption because the cubes we need are much larger. A cube with side 1 µm is a thousand times larger than a nanometre and contains \(1000^3 = 10^9\) cubes with side 1 nm. By the table of chapter 1 (figure 1.6) the quotient of a cube with side \(1000{,}5\) nm, only half a nanometre larger, differs from the density of the matter by at most \(0{,}15\ \%\) wherever we place the cube, even if the spacing of the particles is a whole nanometre. In this way we replace the region full of particles by continuous matter. The density at a point is thus the quotient for cubes that are small compared with the body and large compared with the atoms. For bodies only a few nanometres in size there are no such cubes and the notion fails.

With the density at a point we can write the weight also in a body that is not equally dense everywhere. The cube around \(P\) has the mass \(\Delta m\) and by (2.1) the weight \(g\,\Delta m\). If the axis \(x\) points down,

\[\frac{\Delta\vek F_{\mathrm{V}}}{h^3} = g\,\frac{\Delta m}{h^3}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} , \qquad \text{so} \qquad \vek b(P) = \rho(P)\,g\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} . \tag{2.31}\]

For as the quotient \(\Delta m/h^3\) approaches \(\rho(P)\), its multiple by \(g\) approaches \(g\,\rho(P)\). At the point \(P\) of figure 2.88 the magnitude of \(\vek b\) is \(76\,518\) N/m³, and at every point of the aluminium it is \(26\,487\) N/m³.

2.7.5 The accelerated bar and the inertial term

In the lectures one more term per unit volume stands beside the body force \(\vec f\), namely \(-\rho\,\vec a\), where \(\vec a\) is the acceleration. Where does it come from, and is it a force? Let us look at the bar.

We now pull the steel bar of section 2.7.2 up by its top face so hard that all of it moves up with the acceleration \(a = 5\) m/s² (figure 2.91). The axis \(x\) points down, so the component of the acceleration is \(a_{\mathrm{x}} = -5\) m/s². We assume that the bar moves as a whole, that is, that all its points have the same acceleration at every instant. This holds once the extension of the bar no longer changes in time. Right after a sudden start of the pull, however, the bar vibrates lengthwise and its points are not equally accelerated. We will treat such vibration in chapter 13. For the bar 10 m long the slowest of it has the period \(2L/c = 3{,}99\) ms, the time in which sound with the speed \(c = 5012{,}80\) m/s runs along the steel bar there and back (we pull the top end with a given force, so for this vibration both ends are free, theorem 13.24 (c)). During the vibration the stress inside the bar oscillates about the value we compute below, and once the vibration has died out it equals that value. Without this assumption the acceleration would not be one number for the whole slice, and the calculation below would hold only in the limit of a thin slice.

Let us look at the same slice as before, from the depth \(2L/5\) to the depth \(3L/5\), enlarged in the middle of the figure. The forces on it are of the same kinds as for the bar at rest: the part above pulls it up, the part below pulls it down, the weight acts down. But the slice is not in equilibrium, since it accelerates upwards. It moves as a whole, without turning and without changing shape, so Newton's law of section 2.1 holds for it: the resultant of the forces equals the mass times the acceleration. The mass of the slice is \(\rho A\,\Delta x\), so in the direction \(x\)

\[-\sigma(x - \tfrac{\Delta x}{2})\,A + \sigma(x + \tfrac{\Delta x}{2})\,A + \rho g A\,\Delta x = \rho A\,\Delta x\,a_{\mathrm{x}} . \tag{2.32}\]

We divide the equation by the volume of the slice \(A\,\Delta x\) and move the right side to the left:

\[\frac{\sigma(x + \tfrac{\Delta x}{2}) - \sigma(x - \tfrac{\Delta x}{2})}{\Delta x} + \rho g - \rho\,a_{\mathrm{x}} = 0 . \tag{2.33}\]

Let us compare it with equation (2.28) for the bar at rest. They differ only in that beside the weight per unit volume \(\rho g\) stands one more term, \(-\rho\,a_{\mathrm{x}}\). So the accelerated slice satisfies the same equation as a slice at rest on which, besides the weight, the body force \(-\rho\,\vek a\) acts. This is d'Alembert's view: the term \(-\rho\,\vek a\) is called the inertial force (vztrajnostna sila) per unit volume, and the motion is treated as equilibrium (GR (1.1), PDF p. 32, for a particle. SADD §3.1, PDF p. 63, lists inertial forces among the body forces).

Let us compute. The weight per unit volume is \(\rho g = 76\,518\) N/m³, and the inertial term is \(-\rho\,a_{\mathrm{x}} = 7800 \cdot 5 = 39\,000\) N/m³, together \(115\,518\) N/m³. Let us draw the stress along the bar as in figure 2.24 (figure 2.90). The vertical axis \(x\) shows the depth from the top to the free end at 10 m, and the width of the shape at the depth \(x\) is the stress at that depth. Because of the sum \(115\,518\) N/m³ the stress falls with depth by \(0{,}1155\) MPa per metre instead of by \(0{,}0765\) MPa as for the bar at rest. At the free lower end it is zero, so by the same argument as in section 2.7.2 \(\sigma(x) = \rho\,(g + a)\,(L - x)\), the orange triangle, at the top \(1{,}155\) MPa instead of the \(0{,}765\) MPa of the grey dashed triangle of the bar at rest. On the upper and lower faces of the slice the stresses are \(0{,}6931\) and \(0{,}4621\) MPa, and multiplied by the area \(A = 7{,}854 \cdot 10^{-5}\) m² they give the forces on the slice. The slice is pulled up by \(54{,}44\) N and down by \(36{,}29\) N, and it weighs \(12{,}02\) N. These three forces do not cancel:

\[-54{,}44\ \text{N} + 36{,}29\ \text{N} + 12{,}02\ \text{N} = -6{,}13\ \text{N} .\]

The resultant points up and equals the mass of the slice, \(1{,}225\) kg, times \(a_{\mathrm{x}} = -5\) m/s². On the right is the same slice with the same three forces and with the dashed orange arrow \(-\rho\,\vek a\,A\,\Delta x\), \(6{,}13\) N down. With it the sum is zero: \(54{,}44 = 36{,}29 + 12{,}02 + 6{,}13\).

Is \(-\rho\,\vek a\) a body force by definition 2.28? No. Nothing outside the body acts on the matter with it, which is why it is dashed in the figure. It is a term of Newton's law moved to the other side of the equation. But we compute with it just as with the weight: it is proportional to the mass, it belongs to every bit of matter, and for a slice that moves as a whole we draw it from the centre.

We know the effect from a lift (figure 2.92). Say our mass is 70 kg. In a lift at rest the floor pushes us up with the force \(686{,}7\) N, as large as our weight \(70 \cdot 9{,}81\) N. When the lift starts upwards with the acceleration 5 m/s², our weight stays \(686{,}7\) N, but Newton's law requires the resultant of the forces on us to be \(70 \cdot 5 = 350\) N upwards. So the floor pushes us with \(686{,}7 + 350 = 1036{,}7\) N. We feel this harder push on our soles as if we were heavier. With the inertial term of 350 N downwards the sum of the forces is zero, as for a person at rest with the weight \(70 \cdot 14{,}81 = 1036{,}7\) N. In the same way a bar accelerated upwards with 5 m/s² is stressed just like a bar at rest in a place where the acceleration of gravity is \(g + a = 14{,}81\) m/s² (the orange triangle). In this book \(\vek b\) means only forces with which something acts on the matter, and the acceleration stays on the right side of the equations. We will write them so for a general body in section 2.7.8, and d'Alembert's principle will be proved in chapter 8 (theorem 8.79).

2.7.6 Forces on a small cube

Now take a general body at rest and a point \(P = (x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}}, z_{\mathrm{P}})\) in its interior, in a rectangular Cartesian coordinate system. Around \(P\) we cut out in thought a cube with centre \(P\), side \(h\) and edges parallel to the axes (figure 2.93). Since \(P\) is an interior point, for small enough \(h\) the whole cube lies in the body. Books often take a rectangular box (kvader), a body bounded by six rectangles of which each two opposite ones are equal and parallel. A cube is a box with equal edges. CM takes a box with three different edges (CM (4.5.1), PDF p. 198). We take a cube because its size is given by a single number \(h\). The lectures call such a small cube, shrunk towards the point, an elementary particle (elementarni delec). When we shrink it, we will therefore compute a limit from the right of a function of one number (definition 1.8). The point \(P\) is the centre of the cube so that the cube shrinks towards \(P\) equally from all sides.

The cube has six faces, each perpendicular to one of the axes (figure 2.93). The face on the side of larger \(x\) has the outward normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and the centre \(Q_{+\mathrm{x}} = P + \tfrac h2\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). The opposite face has the outward normal \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and the centre \(Q_{-\mathrm{x}} = P - \tfrac h2\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). In the same way \(Q_{\pm \mathrm{y}} = P \pm \tfrac h2\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(Q_{\pm \mathrm{z}} = P \pm \tfrac h2\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) are the centres of the faces with outward normals \(\pm\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\pm\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). We denote the force with which the rest of the body acts on the cube across the face with outward normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) by \(\Delta\vek F_{+\mathrm{x}}\), the force across the opposite face by \(\Delta\vek F_{-\mathrm{x}}\), and likewise \(\Delta\vek F_{\pm \mathrm{y}}\) and \(\Delta\vek F_{\pm \mathrm{z}}\). The index gives the outward normal of the face, as for the tetrahedron in section 2.6.2. On the matter in the cube acts also the body force \(\Delta\vek F_{\mathrm{V}}\). Is the cube in equilibrium too? The body is at rest, the cube rests with it, and by Newton's second law the resultant of the forces on the cube, which does not accelerate, is the zero vector. The same holds in a body all of whose points move without acceleration. Equilibrium of the body as a whole (definition 2.3), however, is not enough. A plate spinning uniformly about its centre is in equilibrium, but a cube in it moves on a circle. The velocity of the cube has a different direction later than earlier. On the right both velocities are drawn from the same point, their difference from the tip of the first to the tip of the second points towards the centre, and the cube accelerates (figure 2.94). For a cube that accelerates, the mass times the acceleration remains on the right side of the equation, as for the accelerated slice in section 2.7.5, where this term, \(6{,}13\) N, is a good half of the weight of the slice, \(12{,}02\) N. For a cube at rest, by (2.2)

\[\Delta\vek F_{+\mathrm{x}} + \Delta\vek F_{-\mathrm{x}} + \Delta\vek F_{+\mathrm{y}} + \Delta\vek F_{-\mathrm{y}} + \Delta\vek F_{+\mathrm{z}} + \Delta\vek F_{-\mathrm{z}} + \Delta\vek F_{\mathrm{V}} = \vek 0 . \tag{2.34}\]

How large are these forces? Let us first compute them in the hanging bar, where we can (figure 2.95). The bar is made of steel, 10 m long, with diameter 10 mm, it hangs under its own weight and is held in the idealized way, the axis \(x\) points down from the centre of the top face. Take the point \(P = (5\ \text{m}, 4\ \text{mm}, 0)\) from section 1.7.1, at the middle of the length and 1 mm below the surface of the bar, and the cube with centre \(P\) and side \(h = 1\) mm. In the figure the piece of the bar in the frame is drawn to scale, the axis of the bar is dashed, the axes point \(y\) horizontally and \(x\) down, and on the right is the cube enlarged. In the idealized model the only stress component different from zero is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \rho g\,(L - x)\) (CM Example 7.3.2, equation (2), PDF p. 305, where \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = \rho g\,z\) with the axis \(z\) pointing up from the lower end, so \(z = L - x\)). CM takes a bar with a rectangular cross section. The shape of the section does not enter the solution: the stress does not depend on the dimensions of the section, and on the side surface of the bar, where the normal has the component \(x\) equal to zero, Cauchy's formula gives a zero traction vector for every shape of the section. So the solution holds for our round bar too, at least as far as equilibrium goes. That the stress really belongs to some change of shape is a separate question (CM, PDF p. 305). The traction vectors on the faces perpendicular to the axes \(y\) and \(z\) are therefore zero, and there are no forces across the side faces of the cube. On the top face, at the depth \(x_{\mathrm{P}} - h/2\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is the same at all points of the face, so the part of the bar above the cube pulls the cube up with a force of magnitude \(h^2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(Q_{-\mathrm{x}})\). The part of the bar below the cube pulls it down with a force of magnitude \(h^2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(Q_{+\mathrm{x}})\). The weight of the cube is \(\rho g h^3\). With NumPy we computed:

\(h\) force on the top face difference of the forces on the top and the bottom face weight of the cube difference divided by the force on the top face
1 mm \(0{,}3826\) N \(7{,}652 \cdot 10^{-5}\) N \(7{,}652 \cdot 10^{-5}\) N \(2{,}0 \cdot 10^{-4}\)
0,1 mm \(3{,}826 \cdot 10^{-3}\) N \(7{,}652 \cdot 10^{-8}\) N \(7{,}652 \cdot 10^{-8}\) N \(2{,}0 \cdot 10^{-5}\)
0,01 mm \(3{,}826 \cdot 10^{-5}\) N \(7{,}652 \cdot 10^{-11}\) N \(7{,}652 \cdot 10^{-11}\) N \(2{,}0 \cdot 10^{-6}\)

The forces on the top and the bottom face are almost equal and opposite (figure 2.95, right). Their difference is, for \(h = 1\) mm, only two ten-thousandths of each of them, and this difference is exactly the weight of the cube. When we make \(h\) smaller by a factor of 10, the forces on the faces become smaller by approximately a factor of 100, because they are almost proportional to the area \(h^2\) (the stress at the centre of the face changes little with \(h\)). The difference and the weight, however, become smaller by a factor of 1000. Why the difference? The two faces are a distance \(h\) apart, the stress changes between them by \(\rho g h\), and so the difference of the forces is \(\rho g h \cdot h^2 = \rho g h^3\). The weight is proportional to the volume, \(h^3\). Here lies the essential difference from the tetrahedron in section 2.6.2. There the weight was proportional to \(h^3\) and the forces across the faces to \(h^2\), so the weight disappeared for a small tetrahedron. For the cube the two forces across opposite faces almost cancel, what remains is a difference proportional to \(h^3\), and it is as large as the weight. When we divide the equilibrium by the volume \(h^3\), both will remain.

In a general body the traction vectors at different points are different. So far we wrote the traction vector as \(\vek t(\vek n)\) and left the point out, because we computed everything at one point. Now we compare traction vectors at different points, at the centres \(Q_{+\mathrm{x}}\) and \(Q_{-\mathrm{x}}\) of opposite faces of the cube, which are \(h\) apart, so we write the point: \(\vek t(Q, \vek n)\) is the traction vector at the point \(Q\) on a face with unit normal \(\vek n\). SADD also stresses that the traction vector depends on the point and on the normal (SADD §3.2, PDF p. 65). The stress components at every point \(Q\) of the body are nine numbers, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(Q)\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}(Q)\) and so on. As the point \(Q\) runs through the body, we get nine functions of the point, which, like the components of the displacement, we call fields. By (2.26), for example,

\[\vek t(Q, \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) = \big(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(Q),\ \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}(Q),\ \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}(Q)\big) .\]

Figure 2.96 shows the components \(x\) of the forces on all six faces of the cube with side \(h\) in two views, at the top along the axis \(y\) and at the bottom along the axis \(z\) (the drawn axes), as they would be if the traction vector over the whole face were equal to the one at its centre. On the faces with outward normals \(\pm\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) they are the normal components \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) times the area \(h^2\). On the faces with outward normals \(\pm\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) they are the shear components \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\) in the bottom view, the components \(x\) of the traction vector on the face perpendicular to the axis \(y\). On the faces with outward normals \(\pm\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) they are the shear components \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\) in the top view. On the faces with outward normals \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) the components point the opposite ways, because there the traction vector is opposite by lemma 2.21 on the traction on the opposite side of a cut. From \(P\) we also draw the component \(x\) of the body force, \(h^3 b_{\mathrm{x}}\), since \(h^3\) is the volume of the cube.

But how large is the force across a face really? If the traction vector were the same at all points of the face, the force would be the area of the face times it, as for the cross section of a bar. In a general body, however, the traction vector changes a little from point to point of the face. Let us first see what happens when it changes linearly, that is, so that a component, for example \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), changes by \(w\) times a fixed number \(k\) when we move along the face by the distance \(w\) in a chosen direction (figure 2.97, left). Take the face of side \(h\) with outward normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and centre \(Q_{+\mathrm{x}}\). Two points of the face that lie symmetrically about the centre then have the values \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(Q_{+\mathrm{x}}) + k w\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(Q_{+\mathrm{x}}) - k w\). Together they carry as much as two points with the value \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(Q_{+\mathrm{x}})\) would, since \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(Q_{+\mathrm{x}}) + k w) + (\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(Q_{+\mathrm{x}}) - k w) = 2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(Q_{+\mathrm{x}})\). The face splits into such pairs of small patches, symmetric about the centre. So the force is exactly the area times the value at the centre. As much as one half of the face carries more, the other half carries less.

A field that does not change linearly is, however, linear near the point \(P\) up to a small remainder (figure 2.97, right). Let us assume that the stress components are continuously differentiable fields (definition 1.91), that is, that they have partial derivatives which change from point to point without jumps. Physically this means that the stress in the body changes smoothly. Where this assumption fails we saw for displacements in section 1.15: at a concentrated force, at the tip of a crack and at the interface of two materials. What the assumption gives the result: the remainder is small compared with \(h\) in a small cube. At a point where it does not hold there is no such guarantee, and the derivation below does not hold there. By theorem 1.89 on the change of a field over a short step we then have for the component \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\)

\[\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(Q) &= \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(P) + \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial x}(P)\,(x_{\mathrm{Q}} - x_{\mathrm{P}}) \\ &\quad + \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial y}(P)\,(y_{\mathrm{Q}} - y_{\mathrm{P}}) + \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial z}(P)\,(z_{\mathrm{Q}} - z_{\mathrm{P}}) + R(Q) , \end{aligned}\]

where \(Q\) is a point near \(P\), and for every chosen error \(\eta > 0\) the remainder is at most \(\eta\,|PQ|\) when \(Q\) is close enough to \(P\). The sum of the first four terms changes linearly with the coordinates of the point \(Q\). Of the points of the cube, the corners are farthest from \(P\), for example \(P + (\tfrac h2, \tfrac h2, \tfrac h2)\), which by (1.10) is at the distance \(\sqrt{(\tfrac h2)^2 + (\tfrac h2)^2 + (\tfrac h2)^2} = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\,h = 0{,}866\,h\) (figure 2.98, left). This is less than the side \(h\), so in the cube the remainder is less than \(\eta h\). The linear part gives on every face exactly its value at the centre, as we saw above. In figure 2.98, right, one component is on a number line, with the value of the linear part at the centre of the face in the middle. The remainder moves the average over the face by less than \(\eta h\) away from it and also the value at the centre of the face by less than \(\eta h\) away from it. So both lie in the band of width \(2\eta h\) around the linear part, and the average force per unit area differs from the traction vector at the centre of the face by less than \(2\eta h\) in each component. Since \(\eta\) is arbitrarily small, the difference divided by \(h\) is, for small enough \(h\), less than \(2\eta\), so it approaches zero as \(h\) approaches zero.

This argument added up the force on a face from the forces on small patches into which we cut the face, shown by the arrows. The book does not have such exact adding up yet (SADD (3.1.2), PDF p. 64, BOWER, PDF p. 66). We will meet it for functions of one variable in chapter 3 and over a surface and over a body in chapter 4, section 4.2. Until then we take the argument as an assumption on the forces on a small cube. This assumption does not follow from equilibrium alone, it needs a model in which the force across a face is the integral of the traction vector over it (SADD (3.1.2), PDF p. 64). For the face with outward normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) it reads

\[\lim_{\mathrm{h} \to 0^+} \frac1h \left( \frac{\Delta\vek F_{+\mathrm{x}}}{h^2} - \vek t(Q_{+\mathrm{x}}, \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) \right) = \vek 0 , \tag{2.35}\]

and the same for the other five faces, each with its outward normal and its centre. The limit is a limit from the right, since \(h > 0\), and we take it component by component. The vector \(\Delta\vek F_{+\mathrm{x}}/h^2\) is the average force per unit area on the face, and the assumption says that it differs from the traction vector at the centre of the face by so little that the difference, divided by \(h\), approaches zero.

Why exactly so that the difference divided by \(h\) goes to zero? Because the difference between the traction vectors on opposite faces is itself of the size \(h\): the faces are a distance \(h\) apart, and in the hanging bar \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) changed between them by \(\rho g h\), so the forces on the top and the bottom face were different. An error comparable with \(h\) could hide this difference completely. CM takes for the force on each face of the box the stress on the face times the area and says nothing about the error (CM (4.5.1), PDF p. 198). SADD derives the equations by exact adding up over a part of the body and over its surface, and leaves the derivation with a small box to the exercises (SADD §3.7, PDF pp. 77-78).

Now we divide equation (2.34) by the volume of the cube \(h^3\). We group the forces on opposite faces in pairs and write each pair with the two average forces per unit area:

\[\begin{aligned} &\frac1h \Big( \frac{\Delta\vek F_{+\mathrm{x}}}{h^2} + \frac{\Delta\vek F_{-\mathrm{x}}}{h^2} \Big) + \frac1h \Big( \frac{\Delta\vek F_{+\mathrm{y}}}{h^2} + \frac{\Delta\vek F_{-\mathrm{y}}}{h^2} \Big) \\ &\qquad + \frac1h \Big( \frac{\Delta\vek F_{+\mathrm{z}}}{h^2} + \frac{\Delta\vek F_{-\mathrm{z}}}{h^2} \Big) + \frac{\Delta\vek F_{\mathrm{V}}}{h^3} = \vek 0 . \end{aligned} \tag{2.36}\]

The first term says by how much the average forces per unit area on the opposite faces perpendicular to the axis \(x\) fail to cancel, divided by the distance \(h\) between the faces. The second and the third term say the same for the faces perpendicular to the axes \(y\) and \(z\). The last term is the average body force per unit volume in the cube, which by definition 2.28 approaches \(\vek b(P)\).

Where does the first term go as \(h\) approaches zero? By the assumption (2.35) it is close to the vector \(\big(\vek t(Q_{+\mathrm{x}}, \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) + \vek t(Q_{-\mathrm{x}}, -\vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\big)/h\), and by lemma 2.21 this equals \(\big(\vek t(Q_{+\mathrm{x}}, \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) - \vek t(Q_{-\mathrm{x}}, \vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\big)/h\). Its component \(x\), from the normal components on the faces with centres \(Q_{+\mathrm{x}}\) and \(Q_{-\mathrm{x}}\), is

\[\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(x_{\mathrm{P}} + \tfrac h2,\ y_{\mathrm{P}},\ z_{\mathrm{P}}) - \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(x_{\mathrm{P}} - \tfrac h2,\ y_{\mathrm{P}},\ z_{\mathrm{P}})}{h} ,\]

of the same form as the first term of (2.28). It is the difference of the values of a function at two points that lie symmetrically about \(x_{\mathrm{P}}\), divided by the distance between them.

2.7.7 Mathematics: the central difference quotient

We defined the derivative with the difference quotient (1.3), which compares the value of a function at the point \(x\) and at the point \(x + \Delta x\) beside it. For the slice and for the cube, however, the point we care about lies in the middle between the points at which we compare the values. Does such a quotient also approach the derivative? The idea is simple. We split the step from \(x - \tfrac h2\) to \(x + \tfrac h2\) into a step back from \(x\) and a step forward from \(x\). Each gives an ordinary difference quotient, the slope of its half chord, which approaches the derivative, and our quotient, the slope of the whole chord, is their average.

From history

In his Methodus incrementorum directa et inversa, which appeared in the years 1715 to 1717, Brook Taylor created the calculus of finite differences (račun končnih razlik), that is the calculus with differences of function values at points a finite distance apart (CAJORI, PDF p. 242). Among other things he used it for the form of motion of a vibrating string, which he was the first to try to reduce to mechanical principles (CAJORI, PDF p. 242). Euler developed the calculus of finite differences in the first chapters of his book Institutiones calculi differentialis, which appeared in 1755 (CAJORI, PDF p. 249 and 254-255). From it he derived the differential calculus (CAJORI, PDF p. 255). In this section too we reach the derivative by way of differences.

Let us return to the quotient that compares the values of the function at the points \(x - \tfrac h2\) and \(x + \tfrac h2\) around the point \(x\).

Lemma 2.30 Central difference quotient (centralni diferenčni količnik)

Let \(f\) be a function of one variable, defined for all numbers at a distance less than some \(r > 0\) from \(x\), and differentiable at \(x\). Then the central difference quotient (centralni diferenčni količnik) approaches the derivative:

\[\lim_{\mathrm{h} \to 0} \frac{f(x + \tfrac h2) - f(x - \tfrac h2)}{h} = f'(x) . \tag{2.37}\]
Proof

We must show that the quotient on the left approaches the number \(f'(x)\). We will write it as the average of an ordinary difference quotient with a step \(\tfrac h2\) forward and an ordinary difference quotient with a step \(\tfrac h2\) back.

Let us look at the quotient \(q\) as a function of the step. On the horizontal axis is the step \(\Delta x\), the curve shows \(q(\Delta x)\), which is not defined at \(\Delta x = 0\), and the horizontal dashed line is its limit \(f'(x)\). Around it is the error band \(\eta\), and between \(-\delta'\) and \(\delta'\) the curve lies in it.

  1. The function \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\), so the limit of the difference quotient exists (definition 1.9). By the definition of the limit 1.5 the quotient \(q(\Delta x) = \big(f(x + \Delta x) - f(x)\big)/\Delta x\) is therefore defined for all \(\Delta x\) with \(0 < |\Delta x| < r\) for some \(r > 0\), and \(\lim_{\Delta \mathrm{x} \to 0} q(\Delta x) = f'(x)\). So for \(0 < |h| < 2r\) both values \(f(x + \tfrac h2)\) and \(f(x - \tfrac h2)\) are defined.
  2. We subtract and add \(f(x)\) in the numerator of the central quotient and split the fraction into two. In 2.100 this means that we split the rise of the whole chord into the rise of the forward half chord and the rise of the backward half chord:
    \[\frac{f(x + \tfrac h2) - f(x - \tfrac h2)}{h} = \frac{f(x + \tfrac h2) - f(x)}{h} + \frac{f(x) - f(x - \tfrac h2)}{h} .\]
  3. In the denominator of the first fraction \(h = 2 \cdot \tfrac h2\), so the first fraction equals \(\tfrac12 \cdot \big(f(x + \tfrac h2) - f(x)\big)/\tfrac h2 = \tfrac12\,q(\tfrac h2)\).
  4. We multiply the numerator and the denominator of the second fraction by \(-1\). The numerator becomes \(f(x - \tfrac h2) - f(x)\) and the denominator \(-h = 2 \cdot (-\tfrac h2)\). So the second fraction is \(\tfrac12 \cdot \big(f(x - \tfrac h2) - f(x)\big)/(-\tfrac h2) = \tfrac12\,q(-\tfrac h2)\). The central quotient is therefore \(\tfrac12\,q(\tfrac h2) + \tfrac12\,q(-\tfrac h2)\), the average of the quotients with the step forward and back. In 2.100, left, this is the slope of the chord as the average of the slopes of the backward half chord and the forward half chord, for every function, not only for the parabola.
  5. Let us show that \(\lim_{\mathrm{h} \to 0} q(\tfrac h2) = f'(x)\). We choose an error \(\eta > 0\). By step 1 there is a band \(\delta' > 0\) such that \(|q(\Delta x) - f'(x)| < \eta\) for every \(\Delta x\) with \(0 < |\Delta x| < \delta'\). We take \(\delta = 2\delta'\). For every \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < \delta\) we have \(0 < |\tfrac h2| < \delta'\), so \(|q(\tfrac h2) - f'(x)| < \eta\).
  6. In the same way \(\lim_{\mathrm{h} \to 0} q(-\tfrac h2) = f'(x)\), since for \(0 < |h| < \delta\) also \(0 < |{-\tfrac h2}| < \delta'\).
  7. By lemma 2.25 on the limit of a sum with the numbers \(c_1 = c_2 = \tfrac12\) the central quotient approaches the number \(\tfrac12\,f'(x) + \tfrac12\,f'(x) = f'(x)\).

Source: CHK (6.2) (PDF p. 104), where the central difference quotient is an approximation of a partial derivative. The proof is not from the source. The error orders \(h\) and \(h^2\) quoted for the lemma are stated by CHK (PDF pp. 103-104) without a condition, and LEBL1 thm. 4.3.2 (PDF p. 172) is Taylor's theorem with remainder, from which the estimates follow if the second or the third derivative is bounded. The derivation of the estimates is not from the source. The lemma itself asks for less, only differentiability at \(x\), and also claims less, since it speaks only of the limit.

Let us test the lemma on the displacement of the hanging bar, \(u(x) = a\,(2Lx - x^2)\), whose derivative is \(u'(x) = a\,(2L - 2x)\) (section 1.3.4). The numerator of the central quotient is

\[u(x + \tfrac h2) - u(x - \tfrac h2) = a\,\big(2L\,h - (x + \tfrac h2)^2 + (x - \tfrac h2)^2\big) ,\]

because the terms \(2Lx\) cancel and \(2L \cdot \tfrac h2 + 2L \cdot \tfrac h2 = 2L\,h\) remains. We write out the squares as products of brackets: \((x + \tfrac h2)^2 = x^2 + x\,h + \tfrac{h^2}{4}\) and \((x - \tfrac h2)^2 = x^2 - x\,h + \tfrac{h^2}{4}\). Their difference is \(2x\,h\), so the numerator is \(a\,(2L\,h - 2x\,h)\), and divided by \(h\) it gives

\[\frac{u(x + \tfrac h2) - u(x - \tfrac h2)}{h} = a\,(2L - 2x) = u'(x)\]

for every \(h\), not only in the limit. The ordinary difference quotient, by (1.6), was \(a\,(2L - 2x) - a\,\Delta x\) and differed from the derivative by \(a\,\Delta x\). Why is the central quotient exact here? For a parabola the chord between the points above \(x - h/2\) and \(x + h/2\), which lie symmetrically about \(x\), is parallel to the tangent at \(x\) (figure 2.100, left). The chord to \(x + h\), with a step of the same length, is not parallel. For other functions it is not quite parallel, but its slope approaches the slope of the tangent at \(x\) as \(h\) gets smaller, as the lemma says (figure 2.100, right). Because the error of the central quotient shrinks faster than the error of the ordinary one, numerical methods use it as an approximation of the derivative. For functions with a bounded third derivative near \(x\), the error of the ordinary quotient falls like \(h\), the error of the central one like \(h^2\). CHK states this without a condition on the derivatives: the error divided by \(h\) and by \(h^2\) respectively stays bounded (CHK, text before and after (6.2), PDF pp. 103-104). The condition comes from Taylor's theorem with remainder (LEBL1 thm. 4.3.2, PDF p. 172, and theorem 8.68 in chapter 8). If \(|f'''| \le M\) near \(x\), it gives an error of at most \(M h^2/24\) for the central quotient, and for the ordinary quotient a bounded second derivative is enough, \(|f''| \le M_2\), with an error of at most \(M_2 |\Delta x|/2\). Let us test this on \(f(x) = x^3\) at the point \(x = 1\), where \(f'(1) = 3\) (figure 2.101). Since \((1 + h)^3 = 1 + 3h + 3h^2 + h^3\), the ordinary quotient with the step \(h\) equals \(3 + 3h + h^2\), and its error \(3h + h^2\) is drawn on the left as a function of \(h\). For the central quotient, in the difference \((1 + \tfrac h2)^3 - (1 - \tfrac h2)^3\) the terms \(1\) and \(\tfrac34 h^2\) cancel, \(3h + \tfrac{h^3}{4}\) remains, so the quotient is \(3 + \tfrac{h^2}{4}\). Its error \(\tfrac{h^2}{4}\) is drawn on the right, with a vertical scale 16 times larger. When we halve the step from \(0{,}5\) to \(0{,}25\), the error of the ordinary quotient falls from \(1{,}75\) to \(0{,}8125\), a little less than to half, and the error of the central quotient from \(0{,}0625\) to \(0{,}015625\), exactly to a quarter. Here \(f''' = 6\), and the bound \(M h^2/24\) with \(M = 6\) is \(\tfrac{h^2}{4}\), exactly the error. The second derivative \(f''(x) = 6x\) is at most \(M_2 = 6\,(1 + h)\) between \(1\) and \(1 + h\), and the bound \(M_2 h/2 = 3h + 3h^2\) is larger than the error \(3h + h^2\). For a function that is only differentiable at \(x\), the lemma says only that the error goes to zero, not how fast.

The converse does not hold. The function \(f(x) = |x|\) has a graph shaped like the letter V. At the point \(0\) the central chord between the points at \(\pm \tfrac h2\) is horizontal, so the central quotient \(\big(|\tfrac h2| - |{-\tfrac h2}|\big)/h = 0\) for every \(h\) and it approaches zero. But it has no derivative at \(0\), because the ordinary difference quotient \(|\Delta x|/\Delta x\) equals \(1\) for \(\Delta x > 0\), which is the slope of the right half chord, and \(-1\) for \(\Delta x < 0\), which is the slope of the left one. This is why the lemma requires that the derivative exists.

Two more consequences matter for us. First: a partial derivative is the derivative of the function of one variable that we get when we hold the other two variables fixed (definition 1.26). If a function of three variables \(f\) has a partial derivative with respect to \(x\) at the point \(P\), then by the lemma, used at the centres \(Q_{\pm \mathrm{x}}\) of the opposite faces of the cube,

\[\frac{f(x_{\mathrm{P}} + \tfrac h2,\ y_{\mathrm{P}},\ z_{\mathrm{P}}) - f(x_{\mathrm{P}} - \tfrac h2,\ y_{\mathrm{P}},\ z_{\mathrm{P}})}{h}\]

approaches \(\partial f/\partial x\) at \(P\), and likewise with respect to \(y\) and to \(z\). Second: the lemma speaks of the limit as \(h\) goes to zero from both sides. The condition for \(0 < |h| < \delta\) contains the condition for \(0 < h < \delta\), so with the same band the quotient approaches the derivative also from the right. We need this for the cube, where \(h > 0\). For the slice of the hanging bar the lemma says that the first term of (2.28) approaches \(\sigma'(x)\) as \(\Delta x\) goes to zero, when \(\sigma\) is differentiable at \(x\). So by lemma 2.25 on the limit of a sum the left side of (2.28) approaches \(\sigma'(x) + \rho g\). But it is zero for every \(\Delta x\), so by the uniqueness of the limit (lemma 1.7) \(\sigma'(x) + \rho g = 0\).

2.7.8 The equilibrium equations

Now we can let \(h\) approach zero in (2.36). The idea of the proof is this. Each pair of opposite faces, for example the faces with the centres \(Q_{+\mathrm{x}}\) and \(Q_{-\mathrm{x}}\), gives a central difference quotient of the components of a traction vector, which by lemma 2.30 approaches their partial derivatives at \(P\). The error that the assumption on the forces on the faces allows disappears on the way. The last term approaches the body force \(\vek b(P)\). The left side is the zero vector for every \(h\), so the sum of the limits is the zero vector too.

The theorem lists exactly the assumptions that the proof uses. The body must be at rest or none of its points may accelerate, because the equilibrium of the body as a whole is not enough: a cube in a uniformly spinning plate accelerates, although the plate is in equilibrium (section 2.7.6). For an accelerating cube the equations get a new term, which for the accelerated slice was a good half of its weight (sections 2.7.6 and 2.7.9). Assumption 1 holds when the stress components are continuously differentiable fields. Assumption 2 holds for the weight when the density at the point exists at \(P\) ((2.31)). Assumption 3 we justified by the argument about the linear part of the field, which in chapter 4 we will write with an integral, when the force across a face is the integral of the traction vector over it. Assumption 4 is the model of forces in a body from section 2.7.6: the neighbouring matter acts on the cube only across shared faces, and everything else acts on all its matter as a body force. It fails when a force at a single point acts inside the cube, as we show after the theorem.

Assumption 3 below says how well the traction vector at the centre of a face replaces the average over the face. The face is a square of side \(h\), and the traction vector varies over it, as the grey arrows show. At the centre \(Q_{+\mathrm{x}}\) it has a value, and the average over the face is slightly different. The difference shrinks much faster than the side when the face gets smaller, as the right face of side \(\tfrac h2\) shows.

Theorem 2.31 Equilibrium equations (ravnotežne enačbe)

Let a body be at rest or let none of its points accelerate, let \(P = (x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}}, z_{\mathrm{P}})\) be a point in its interior and \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) the axes of a rectangular Cartesian coordinate system. For \(h > 0\) we consider the cube with centre \(P\), side \(h\) and edges parallel to the axes. Assume:

  1. The stress components have partial derivatives with respect to \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) at the point \(P\).
  2. The body force density \(\vek b(P) = (b_{\mathrm{x}}, b_{\mathrm{y}}, b_{\mathrm{z}})\) exists at the point \(P\) (definition 2.28).
  3. On every face of the cube the average force per unit area, that is, the force across the face divided by the area \(h^2\), differs from the traction vector at the centre of the face by so little that the difference, divided by \(h\), approaches zero as \(h\) approaches zero. For the face with outward normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) this means
    \[\lim_{\mathrm{h} \to 0^+} \frac1h \left( \frac{\Delta\vek F_{+\mathrm{x}}}{h^2} - \vek t(Q_{+\mathrm{x}}, \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) \right) = \vek 0 ,\]
    where \(\Delta\vek F_{+\mathrm{x}}\) is the force with which the rest of the body acts on the cube across this face, \(Q_{+\mathrm{x}} = P + \tfrac h2\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) is the centre of the face, and \(\vek t(Q, \vek n)\) is the traction vector at the point \(Q\) on a face with unit normal \(\vek n\). The limit is a limit from the right, taken component by component. The same holds for the faces with outward normals \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\pm\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\pm\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) and centres \(Q_{-\mathrm{x}} = P - \tfrac h2\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(Q_{\pm \mathrm{y}} = P \pm \tfrac h2\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(Q_{\pm \mathrm{z}} = P \pm \tfrac h2\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\).
  4. The only forces on the cube are the forces \(\Delta\vek F_{+\mathrm{x}}\), \(\Delta\vek F_{-\mathrm{x}}\), \(\Delta\vek F_{\pm \mathrm{y}}\) and \(\Delta\vek F_{\pm \mathrm{z}}\) with which the rest of the body acts on it across its six faces, and the body force \(\Delta\vek F_{\mathrm{V}}\) on the matter in it.

Then at the point \(P\)

\[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}}{\partial z} + b_{\mathrm{x}} &= 0 , \\ \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}}{\partial z} + b_{\mathrm{y}} &= 0 , \\ \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}}{\partial z} + b_{\mathrm{z}} &= 0 , \end{aligned} \tag{2.38}\]
\[\sigma_{\mathrm{ji},\mathrm{j}} + b_{\mathrm{i}} = 0 , \qquad i = x, y, z , \tag{2.38}\]

where all the partial derivatives are taken at the point \(P\).

Proof

We must show three equalities at the point \(P\). We get them all at once, as the three components of one vector equality. We divide the equilibrium of the cube by its volume and let \(h\) approach zero.

  1. The point \(P\) is in the interior of the body, so for small enough \(h\) the whole cube lies in the body. The body is at rest or none of its points accelerates, so no point of the cube accelerates, and by Newton's second law the resultant of the forces on the cube is the zero vector (section 2.7.6). By assumption 4 these are the forces across the six faces and the body force, so (2.34) holds. This is the first condition of equilibrium of definition 2.3, written for the cube.
  2. We divide the equation by the volume of the cube \(h^3\) and group the forces on opposite faces in pairs. We get (2.36), which holds for every small enough \(h > 0\).
  3. In the first term of (2.36) we subtract and add the traction vector \(\vek t(Q_{+\mathrm{x}}, \vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\) at the centre \(Q_{+\mathrm{x}}\) of this face to the vector \(\Delta\vek F_{+\mathrm{x}}/h^2\), and \(\vek t(Q_{-\mathrm{x}}, -\vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\) at the centre \(Q_{-\mathrm{x}}\) of the opposite face to the vector \(\Delta\vek F_{-\mathrm{x}}/h^2\). By the rules of calculation with vectors (lemma 1.15) the first term equals
    \[\frac{\vek t(Q_{+\mathrm{x}}, \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) + \vek t(Q_{-\mathrm{x}}, -\vek e_{\mathrm{x}})}{h} + \frac1h \Big( \frac{\Delta\vek F_{+\mathrm{x}}}{h^2} - \vek t(Q_{+\mathrm{x}}, \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) \Big) + \frac1h \Big( \frac{\Delta\vek F_{-\mathrm{x}}}{h^2} - \vek t(Q_{-\mathrm{x}}, -\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) \Big) .\]
  4. By assumption 3 the last two vectors of step 3 approach the zero vector as \(h\) approaches zero.
  5. By lemma 2.21 on the traction on the opposite side of a cut, \(\vek t(Q_{-\mathrm{x}}, -\vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\) \(= -\vek t(Q_{-\mathrm{x}}, \vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\). So the first vector of step 3 is \(\big(\vek t(Q_{+\mathrm{x}}, \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) - \vek t(Q_{-\mathrm{x}}, \vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\big)/h\). By (2.26) its components are
    \[\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(Q_{+\mathrm{x}}) - \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(Q_{-\mathrm{x}})}{h} , \qquad \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}(Q_{+\mathrm{x}}) - \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}(Q_{-\mathrm{x}})}{h} , \qquad \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}(Q_{+\mathrm{x}}) - \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}(Q_{-\mathrm{x}})}{h} .\]
  6. The points \(Q_{\pm \mathrm{x}}\) \(= (x_{\mathrm{P}} \pm \tfrac h2,\ y_{\mathrm{P}},\ z_{\mathrm{P}})\) lie on the line through the centre \(P\) parallel to the axis \(x\), each \(\tfrac h2\) from \(P\), so they differ from \(P\) only in the coordinate \(x\). Each component of step 5 is therefore the central difference quotient of a function of one variable, for example \(s \mapsto \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(s, y_{\mathrm{P}}, z_{\mathrm{P}})\), at the point \(x_{\mathrm{P}}\). The derivative of this function at \(x_{\mathrm{P}}\) is the partial derivative \(\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/\partial x\) at \(P\) (definition 1.26), which exists by assumption 1. By lemma 2.30 on the central difference quotient the components therefore approach \(\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/\partial x\), \(\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}/\partial x\) and \(\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}/\partial x\) at \(P\). The lemma speaks of the limit from both sides, so it holds also for the right-hand limit.
  7. By lemma 2.25 on the limit of a sum, used on each component separately, the first term of (2.36) therefore approaches, by steps 3 to 6, the vector
    \[\Big( \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial x},\ \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x},\ \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}}{\partial x} \Big) .\]
  8. We treat the second and the third term in the same way. The points \(Q_{\pm \mathrm{y}}\) differ from \(P\) only in the coordinate \(y\), the points \(Q_{\pm \mathrm{z}}\) only in the coordinate \(z\), and the components of the vectors \(\vek t(Q, \vek e_{\mathrm{y}})\) and \(\vek t(Q, \vek e_{\mathrm{z}})\) are \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\). So the second term approaches the vector \((\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}/\partial y,\ \partial\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}/\partial y,\ \partial\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}/\partial y)\) and the third the vector \((\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}/\partial z,\ \partial\sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}/\partial z,\ \partial\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}/\partial z)\).
  9. The last term \(\Delta\vek F_{\mathrm{V}}/h^3\) approaches the vector \(\vek b(P)\) by assumption 2 and definition 2.28.
  10. By the lemma on the limit of a sum the left side of (2.36) approaches the sum of the four vectors of steps 7, 8 and 9. The left side is the zero vector for every small enough \(h\), so its limit is the zero vector. By the uniqueness of the limit (lemma 1.7), which also holds for the limit from the right (step 5 of the proof of lemma 2.21), the two limits are equal:
    \[\Big( \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}}{\partial x} \Big) + \Big( \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}}{\partial y}, \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}}{\partial y}, \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}}{\partial y} \Big) + \Big( \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}}{\partial z}, \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}}{\partial z}, \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}}{\partial z} \Big) + \vek b(P) = \vek 0 .\]
  11. Vectors are added component by component (definition 1.14). The component \(x\) of this equality is the first equation of (2.38), the component \(y\) the second, the component \(z\) the third.

Source: CM (4.5.1)-(4.5.5) (PDF p. 198), with the indices swapped, SADD (3.7.4), (3.7.5) (PDF p. 78), BOWER §2.3.1 (PDF pp. 76-77). Assumption 3 and the proof with the central difference quotient are not from the sources.

What do the equations mean? Each is the first condition of equilibrium, written per unit volume at a single point. The sum of the first three terms is the limit of the force with which the neighbouring matter acts on a cube around \(P\), divided by the volume of the cube, as the cube shrinks to \(P\). It is the part of the forces on opposite faces that does not cancel. The fourth term is the body force per unit volume. So the stress cannot change from point to point in any way at all. Where there is no body force, the changes in the three directions must balance each other: if, for example, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) grows in the direction of the axis \(x\), then \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\) must fall in the direction of the axis \(y\) or \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\) in the direction of the axis \(z\) (figure 2.104).

Let us see this in numbers. We look at a cube of side \(h\) without body force along the axis \(z\), the axis \(x\) points to the right, the axis \(y\) up. Only the components \(x\) of the forces per unit area at the centres of the faces are drawn. On the right face \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 12\) MPa, on the left one \(10\) MPa, so the faces perpendicular to the axis \(x\) together give a surplus of \(2\) MPa in the direction \(+x\), multiplied by the area \(h^2\). On the top face \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = 3\) MPa, on the bottom one \(5\) MPa. The bottom face has the outward normal \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), so its component \(x\) points in the direction \(-x\) (lemma 2.21), and the faces perpendicular to the axis \(y\) give a deficit of \(2\) MPa. On the front and the back face let \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\) be the same, so their contributions cancel. The sum of the components \(x\) is zero, as the equilibrium of the cube requires.
