The differences divided by the distance \(h\) between opposite faces are central difference quotients, which approach \(\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/\partial x\) and \(\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}/\partial y\) as the cube shrinks, and their sum \(2\ \text{MPa}/h - 2\ \text{MPa}/h = 0\) is the first equation of (2.38) with \(b_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\).

The pattern of the indices is worth noticing. In the equation for the component \(x\) all the stress components have the second index \(x\), because they are the components \(x\) of the traction vectors on the three faces. Each is differentiated with respect to the coordinate named by its first index, that is, in the direction of the normal of its face, since the two opposite faces are a distance apart in exactly this direction, like the faces with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\) in the direction \(y\). With the indices \(i\) and \(j\) running over \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\), and with \(x_{\mathrm{j}}\) for the coordinate named \(j\) (\(x_{\mathrm{x}} = x\), \(x_{\mathrm{y}} = y\), \(x_{\mathrm{z}} = z\)), as in section 1.17.1, all three equations can be written as

\[\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{ji}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} + b_{\mathrm{i}} = 0 , \qquad i = x, y, z ,\]

where \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}}\) is, as in section 1.16.2, the sum of three terms, one for each of \(j = x\), \(j = y\) and \(j = z\). Index notation, which the toolbar button Index notation shows at equations (2.38), writes the same sum more briefly, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ji},\mathrm{j}} + b_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\): the comma before the index \(j\) means the partial derivative with respect to \(x_{\mathrm{j}}\), and the sign \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}}\) is left out, because an index \(j\) that appears twice in a term means, by convention, the sum over \(j\). This is how SADD writes the equilibrium equations, with the letter \(F_{\mathrm{i}}\) for \(b_{\mathrm{i}}\) (SADD (3.7.4), (3.7.5), PDF p. 78), and how BOWER writes them, with the force per unit mass (BOWER, PDF pp. 76-77). CM has the indices swapped, \(\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} + \rho_0 f_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\), because in CM \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\) means the component \(i\) on the face perpendicular to the axis \(j\) (CM (4.5.5), PDF p. 198). When we show in the next section that \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}\), this difference will disappear.

Where do the equations hold? At interior points of a body that is at rest or whose points move without acceleration, where the assumptions of the theorem hold. On the surface of the body we do not write them, because a cube around a point of the surface does not lie in the body. There the traction vector is set by the force of the surroundings per unit area (section 2.5). The point \(P\) just below a concentrated force, however, is an interior point, and the cube around it does not contain the point where the force acts. In the plane model of a concentrated force the stress is unbounded only at that point itself, elsewhere it is given by a formula that changes smoothly from point to point, and just below the point of action the stress is large (SADD §8.4.7, (8.4.34), PDF pp. 200-201). So the equations hold at \(P\). The point of action is a point of the surface, where we do not write the equations anyway.

At some interior points, however, the assumptions of the theorem fail (figure 2.106). A force \(\vek F\) acting at the point \(P\) itself is an idealization, like a concentrated force on the surface, since no force really acts at a single point (SADD §5.8, PDF p. 120). At it assumption 4 fails. Besides the forces across the faces, the force \(\vek F\) acts on the cube around \(P\) and adds the term \(\vek F/h^3\) to (2.36). For a force of size \(1\) N and \(h = 1\) mm the size of this term is \(10^9\) N/m³, about \(13\,000\) times the weight of steel per unit volume, \(76\,518\) N/m³. As \(h\) gets smaller, the term grows without bound, so the limit does not exist. At the tip of a crack the stresses grow without bound (SADD §10.8, PDF p. 321), so at a point on the tip the partial derivatives of the stress do not exist and assumption 1 fails.

At the interface of two materials the partial derivatives do not exist in general. Take a hanging bar, held in the idealized way as in section 2.7.6, which is steel at the top and aluminium at the bottom, both halves 5 m long, with the axis \(x\) pointing down. The stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) in a cross-section is the weight of the part of the bar below the cross-section divided by the area of the cross-section. So with the depth \(x\) it falls, per metre by the weight of one metre of the bar divided by the area, that is, by the weight per unit volume of the material in the cross-section ((2.31)). In steel the slope is \(-76\,518\) N/m³, in aluminium \(-26\,487\) N/m³. At the point \(P\) on the interface the graph has a kink: the derivative from the steel side is \(-76\,518\) N/m³, from the aluminium side \(-26\,487\) N/m³, so \(\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/\partial x\) does not exist at \(P\) and the equations do not hold there in this form. Above the interface and below it they do hold, each with its own density: there the first equation is \(\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/\partial x + \rho g = 0\).

Let us also say what the equations cannot do. For nine stress components there are only three equations, and after the next section only three for six different components. In 2.104 the first equation only says that the surplus and the deficit cancel, not how large each of them is. So on their own they do not determine the stress. The missing equations come from the properties of the material, which relate stresses and strains (chapter 3), and from the requirement that the strains fit together (section 1.18).

2.7.9 Three tests

The hanging bar. A steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m hangs under its own weight, held in the idealized way, the axis \(x\) points down from the centre of the top face. The only stress component that is not zero is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \rho g\,(L - x)\) (CM Example 7.3.2, equation (2), PDF p. 305), and the body force is the weight, \(\vek b = \rho g\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). In the first equation of (2.38), \(\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/\partial x = -\rho g\), since \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is a linear function of \(x\) with slope \(-\rho g\). The components \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\) are zero, so their derivatives are zero too. The first equation reads \(-\rho g + 0 + 0 + \rho g = 0\) and holds. On the small cube this means that the force on the top face, pointing up, exceeds the force on the bottom face, pointing down, by exactly the weight of the cube. The term \(-\rho g\) is this difference of the face forces per unit volume, the term \(\rho g\) the weight per unit volume. In the second and the third equation all the stress components are zero and \(b_{\mathrm{y}} = b_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), so they read \(0 = 0\). So the stress in the hanging bar satisfies the equilibrium equations at every interior point.

The equations can do more than check. CM finds the stress in the hanging bar with them (CM Example 7.3.2, PDF p. 305). Let us assume only, as CM does in its assumption (7.3.17), that the only stress component that is not zero is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), and that it depends only on the depth, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = S(x)\). Let the function \(S\) be continuous on \([0, L]\) and differentiable at every point of \((0, L)\).

Why may we assume this? The mantle of the bar and its lower end are free, and the top face is pulled by a force that points only up. Nothing holds the bar sideways, so it can get thinner freely, and CM concludes from this that the other stress components do not arise (CM, PDF p. 305). The pull on the top face and the weight are spread uniformly over the cross-section, so we also guess that \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is the same over the whole cross-section. The assumption is a guess that we must check. The steps below show that with it the equilibrium equations hold. CM also checks that the stress found belongs to some change of shape of the bar (CM, PDF p. 305), and we will compute this change of shape in chapter 3. The assumption fails near a real ceiling to which the bar is welded over its whole top face. In the idealized model the edge of the top face moves towards the axis by \(5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-9}\) m, but the weld does not allow this, so other components arise there. Far from the ceiling the stress is nearly the same (section 1.7.1, SADD §5.6, PDF pp. 114-115). Continuity of \(S\) on the closed interval \([0, L]\) is needed in steps 4 and 5, which use the value \(S(L)\) at the lower end.

The figure shows where we are going. On the horizontal axis is the depth \(x\) from \(0\) to \(L\), on the vertical one the stress. The function \(S\) will turn out to be a straight line falling from \(\rho g L\) at the top to zero at the lower end of the bar. The function \(S(x) + \rho g\,x\) is a horizontal line at the height \(\rho g L\), because its derivative is zero everywhere. The steps below show why.

  1. The second and the third equation hold, because all their terms are zero: on the cube the forces act only along the axis \(x\).
  2. The first equation reads \(S'(x) + \rho g = 0\) for every \(x\) in \((0, L)\): the force on the top face and the force on the bottom face differ by the weight of the cube.
  3. The function \(x \mapsto S(x) + \rho g\,x\) has, by the rules of differentiation (lemma 1.82), the derivative \(S'(x) + \rho g\), which by step 2 is zero at every point of \((0, L)\), so its graph has a horizontal tangent everywhere. The function is continuous on \([0, L]\), because \(S\) and \(\rho g\,x\) are continuous there (corollary 1.65).
  4. By corollary 1.86 on a function with zero derivative, therefore, the function is constant, \(S(x) + \rho g\,x = S(L) + \rho g L\) for every \(x\) in \([0, L]\).
  5. The lower end of the bar is free, so the stress there is zero, \(S(L) = 0\).
  6. From \(S(x) + \rho g\,x = \rho g L\) follows \(S(x) = \rho g\,(L - x)\).

This is the stress of section 2.2. There we got it from the equilibrium of the part of the bar below the cut, here from the equilibrium of every small cube.

Pure shear. Take the cube of section 2.6.6, in which \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} = \tau_0\) at every point and all other stress components are zero. There we did not take the weight into account, so \(\vek b = \vek 0\). All the stress components are the same at all points, so all their partial derivatives are zero, and each of the three equations reads \(0 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 0\). The forces on opposite faces of a small cube cancel exactly here (figure 2.77).

And if we do not neglect the weight? Figure 2.108 shows the same cube from the front, with the axis \(x\) to the right and the axis \(z\) up, and the forces along the faces of size \(\tau_0\) per unit area. Let the cube be made of steel, with density \(\rho = 7800\) kg/m³ and side \(h = 10\) mm. With the axis \(z\) pointing up, \(\vek b = -\rho g\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), the weight of the cube points down, and the third equation requires \(\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}/\partial x + \partial\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}/\partial y + \partial\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}/\partial z = \rho g\). The stress then cannot be the same everywhere. If only \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) changed, it would have to change from the bottom to the top face by \(\rho g \cdot 0{,}01\ \text{m} = 765\) Pa. The upward force on the top face would then be larger by 765 Pa per unit area than the downward force on the bottom face. On a face with area \(h^2 = 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2\) this is \(765\ \text{Pa} \cdot 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2 = 0{,}0765\) N, exactly the weight of the cube \(\rho g h^3 = 7800 \cdot 9{,}81 \cdot 10^{-6}\) N. On the right are both stresses on three segments. The first is \(\tau_0 = 50\) MPa long. Its start, the first 500 kPa, is magnified a hundred times on the second, the start of the second, the first 5 kPa, a hundred times again on the third, and only there can 765 Pa be seen. This is \(1{,}5 \cdot 10^{-5}\) of the stress \(\tau_0 = 50\) MPa, so neglecting the weight was justified.

Water at rest. Water is at rest in a container shaped like a box. The axis \(x\) points vertically down from the water surface, the axes \(y\) and \(z\) are horizontal and parallel to the sides of the bottom of the container. Water has the density \(\rho = 1000\) kg/m³ (VK appendix A.4, PDF p. 637), and the body force is the weight, \(\vek b = \rho g\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). In section 2.6.6 we saw that at every point of a fluid at rest the pressure \(p\) is the same in all directions, so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = -p\), and the shear components are zero. The pressure can, however, be different at different points, \(p = p(Q)\). Let us assume that it is continuously differentiable inside the water. Why may we? Without the partial derivatives we may not even write the equations (assumption 1 of theorem 2.31). The places where the equations fail (a point force, the tip of a crack, the contact of two materials) do not occur inside water at rest. The assumption does not change the result, it only allows the calculation, and we check it at the end: the pressure we obtain is linear in \(x\) and so indeed continuously differentiable. The equilibrium equations read

\[-\frac{\partial p}{\partial x} + \rho g = 0 , \qquad -\frac{\partial p}{\partial y} = 0 , \qquad -\frac{\partial p}{\partial z} = 0 .\]

So the pressure does not change in the horizontal direction and grows downwards at the rate \(\rho g\). What is it, then?

The figure shows the path of step 3. The container is a box, the water surface is its top face. In the water lie two arbitrary points \(A\) and \(B\). From \(A\) goes a segment along the axis \(x\), from there a segment along the axis \(y\) and finally a segment along the axis \(z\), arriving at \(B\). On each of the three \(f\) is constant. The segment from \(A\) up to the surface tells how large this constant value is.

  1. The function \(f = p - \rho g\,x\) has the partial derivatives \(\partial f/\partial x = \partial p/\partial x - \rho g = 0\), \(\partial f/\partial y = 0\) and \(\partial f/\partial z = 0\) at every interior point of the water.
  2. On a segment in the water parallel to the axis \(x\), \(f\) is a function of one variable with zero derivative. Since it is differentiable, it is also continuous (lemma 1.80), so by corollary 1.86 on a function with zero derivative it is constant on the segment. Likewise on segments parallel to the axes \(y\) and \(z\).
  3. In a container shaped like a box, any two interior points of the water can be joined by three such segments, first along the axis \(x\), then \(y\), then \(z\), which do not leave the water. Every coordinate of the two corners of the path equals a coordinate of \(A\) or of \(B\), so the corners lie in the water, since the walls of the container are parallel to the axes. So \(f\) has the same value \(c\) at all interior points of the water. The box shape only makes the path simple. The conclusion holds in every container in which any two points of the water can be joined by a broken line of such segments that does not leave the water. If the water is not connected, for example in two separate containers, \(c\) can have a different value in each container.
  4. At the surface, at \(x = 0\), the air presses on the water with the pressure \(p_0\). If the pressure changes continuously from the point \(A\) up to the surface, then \(c = p_0\).
  5. Therefore the graph of the pressure is a straight line:
    \[p = p_0 + \rho g\,x .\]

This is the law of hydrostatics: the pressure in water at rest grows linearly with depth. The term \(\rho g\,x\) is the weight of the column of water of height \(x\) above a unit area, since such a column has the volume \(x\) times the unit area. CM writes, for a fluid in which the stress is \(-p\) in all directions, the equations of motion in a form which for a fluid at rest gives the same three equations (CM (5.3.14), PDF p. 228). Figure 2.110 shows why it is so. The water is in the container up to the surface, the axis \(x\) points down. The small cube of water with centre \(P\) is hugely enlarged. The water pushes up on the bottom face of the cube harder than it pushes down on the top face, and the difference is exactly the weight of the cube. On the side faces, left and right, it pushes equally. On the right is the graph of the pressure: the straight line starts at the air pressure \(p_0\) at the surface. For water the slope of the line is \(\rho g = 1000 \cdot 9{,}81 = 9810\) N/m³. At the depth 10 m the pressure is \(98\,100\) Pa higher than at the surface, which is about as much as the pressure of the air, about 100 kPa (VK appendix A.4, PDF p. 637). So every 10 m of water adds about one atmosphere of pressure.

Let us compare with the hanging bar (figure 2.111). On the horizontal axis is the depth \(x\) from 0 to 10 m, on the vertical one \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) in kPa. In the steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \rho g\,(L - x)\), in the water \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = -(p_0 + \rho g\,x)\). In both cases the graph is a straight line that falls with depth at the rate \(\rho g\), where \(\rho\) is the density of the material: in the bar the tension gets smaller, in the water the pressure gets larger. The rates are not equal, though. For steel with density 7800 kg/m³, \(\rho g = 76\,518\) N/m³, for water \(\rho g = 9810\) N/m³, 7,8 times less, so the line of the water is flatter. The two lines also differ in where the stress is known. In the bar it is zero at the free lower end, in the water it is \(-p_0\) at the surface.

A body that moves. When a body accelerates, different bits of the cube need not have the same acceleration. By Newton's law for a collection of bits of matter, the resultant of the forces on the cube is the sum of the masses of the bits times their accelerations (section 2.6.4, CM (5.3.6), (5.3.9), PDF p. 227). If the density near \(P\) is constant, \(\rho\), the mass of the cube is \(\rho h^3\). If the acceleration changes continuously from point to point, this sum differs from \(\rho h^3\) times the acceleration of the point \(P\) by so little that the difference divided by \(h^3\) goes to zero. A constant density is not necessary. If the density changes continuously, the mass of the cube divided by \(h^3\) approaches the density \(\rho(P)\) at the point \(P\), and we get the same equation with \(\rho(P)\). At the contact of two materials the density jumps, but there the equations in this form fail anyway. After dividing by \(h^3\), on the right side instead of zero there remains \(\rho\) times the acceleration of the point \(P\). The equilibrium equations then become the equations of motion (enačbe gibanja), for example

\[\frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}}{\partial z} + b_{\mathrm{x}} = \rho\,a_{\mathrm{x}} ,\]

where \(a_{\mathrm{x}}\) is the component \(x\) of the acceleration (BOWER §2.3.1, PDF p. 76, CM (5.3.12), PDF p. 228). We will need them for vibrations of bodies.

The figure shows a cube of side \(h\). In it are several bits of matter, each with its own acceleration, differing only slightly from its neighbours. The acceleration at the centre \(P\) is the one by which we multiply the mass of the cube.

Equilibrium of a finite part of a body. We got the equilibrium equations from the equilibrium of every small cube. Does the converse hold too, that from the equations at every point follows that the resultant of the forces on the body or on any of its parts is zero (the first condition of equilibrium)? We can picture a part of the body as built from small cubes, like a wall from bricks. The two forces across the common face of two neighbouring cubes are opposite by lemma 2.21 on the traction on the opposite side of a cut, so they cancel in the sum. What remains are the forces on the outer surface of the part and the body forces. To make this sum exact we need exact adding up over a surface and over a body, which we will meet in chapter 4, and there we will also show this, in section 4.2.13. The second condition of equilibrium also needs the symmetry of the stress from the next section. SADD goes along this route in the opposite direction, from the equilibrium of any part of the body to the equations at a point (SADD (3.7.1)-(3.7.4), PDF pp. 77-78).

The figure shows a part of the body divided into small cubes. On the common face of two neighbouring cubes one force points one way, the other the opposite way, so they cancel. What remains are the forces on the outer surface and the body forces, the weight of each cube.

The equilibrium equations are the first condition of equilibrium, written at every point of the body. The second condition, that the forces do not turn the body, is still waiting. We will write it on the same small cube in the next section, once we say with numbers how strongly a force tries to turn a body. It will answer the third question from the end of section 2.6: whether \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) equals \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\).
